title: Virtual Memory
summary: How the CPU gives every process its own private, huge address space — and the hardware tricks (pages, page tables, TLB) that make it fast.

blocks.markdown:
**Virtual memory** gives each process its own private address space, separate from physical RAM.

- Every process thinks it owns a huge, contiguous memory — it doesn't.
- The **MMU** (memory management unit, hardware in the CPU) translates each access on the fly.
- This buys **isolation** and lets total program size exceed physical RAM.
- This card covers the CPU/MMU hardware view — OS-side policy is a separate topic.

Without it, every program would touch raw physical RAM directly — fragile and unsafe.

- **Isolation**: one process can't read or corrupt another's memory (or the OS's).
- **Illusion of size**: a process can use more memory than physically installed; unused parts live on disk.
- Each process gets a **private address space** starting at 0, regardless of where it actually lives in RAM.

Two address spaces exist at once, and hardware bridges them.

- **Virtual address** — what the running program uses; made up, private to that process.
- **Physical address** — the real location in RAM chips.
- Every memory access a CPU makes is a virtual address that gets **translated** to physical before RAM sees it.

Translating one byte at a time would be too slow, so memory is chunked.

- A **page** is a fixed-size block of virtual memory (commonly 4 KB).
- A **page frame** is a same-size block of physical RAM.
- Translation maps a whole page to a whole frame at once — one lookup covers thousands of bytes.

The **page table** is the map: one entry per virtual page, pointing to its physical frame.

- Each process has its **own** page table — same virtual address, different physical spot per process.
- An entry also stores flags: **valid**, **read/write**, **present in RAM or not**.
- Kept in RAM itself; the CPU has a register pointing to the current process's table.

Every memory access walks this path before touching RAM.

- Fast path: **TLB hit** — translation already cached.
- Slower path: **TLB miss** — walk the page table in RAM.
- Slowest path: **page fault** — the page isn't in RAM at all, fetch from disk.

blocks.subTitle: What it is
blocks.markdown:
The **TLB (translation lookaside buffer)** is a small, fast cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations, sitting inside the MMU.

- Without it, **every** memory access needs a page table walk in RAM — extra RAM trips for every load and store.
- With a TLB hit, translation takes about one cycle, no RAM walk needed.
- Works because of **locality**: programs reuse the same few pages repeatedly.

blocks.subTitle: Why it matters
blocks.markdown:
A **TLB miss** is costly: the MMU must walk the page table (one or more RAM reads) before it even gets the physical address.

- On a process switch, old translations may no longer be valid — the TLB is often flushed or tagged per-process.
- TLB size is small (dozens to a few thousand entries), so it only covers the **hottest** pages.
- Related idea: [cache-fundamentals](cache-fundamentals) — TLB is a cache, just for translations instead of data.

A **page fault** fires when the page table entry says the page isn't currently in RAM.

- The CPU traps to the OS, which fetches the page from disk into a free frame, updates the page table, then retries the instruction.
- **Demand paging**: pages load only when first touched, not all upfront — keeps startup fast and RAM usage lean.
- A page fault is far slower than a TLB miss — it involves disk I/O, not just RAM.

Page table entries also carry **permission bits**, so translation doubles as a guard.

- Flags like read-only, writable, and executable are checked on every access.
- Writing to a read-only page, or executing a non-executable one, triggers a hardware **fault** — not silent corruption.
- This is how one buggy process can't scribble over another process's memory or the kernel's.

blocks.subTitle: What and why
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is virtual memory, and why do we need it?**

It's an abstraction where each process gets its own private address space, translated to physical RAM by the MMU. It gives **isolation** between processes and lets a process use more memory than physically exists, since inactive pages can live on disk.

blocks.subTitle: Virtual vs physical address
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Difference between a virtual and a physical address?**

A virtual address is what the program uses — private to that process, starting from 0. A physical address is the real location in RAM. The MMU translates virtual to physical on every access, using the page table.

blocks.subTitle: The page table
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a page table and what does it store?**

A per-process map from virtual pages to physical frames. Each entry also holds flags — valid, read/write, present-in-RAM — so it doubles as the source of truth for both translation and protection.

blocks.subTitle: The TLB
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the TLB and why does it speed things up?**

The TLB is a small hardware cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations inside the MMU. Without it, every access needs a page table walk in RAM. A TLB hit skips that walk entirely, cutting translation to about one cycle — it works because programs reuse a small set of pages.

blocks.subTitle: Page faults
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What happens on a page fault?**

The CPU finds the page table entry marked "not present," traps to the OS, which loads the page from disk into a free frame, updates the page table, and retries the instruction. It's slow because it involves disk I/O, unlike a plain TLB miss.
